transcript:
Header:
Date: 2028-08-15
Start: 14:00 PDT
Duration: 52 minutes
Attendees: Maya Thompson (Redwood AE), Liam Chen (Redwood SE), Ravi Patel (Cascade Head of ML), Sophie Martinez (Cascade Platform Eng), Diego Alvarez (Cascade CTO)

Auto-summary (AI): investigating integration approaches for Redwood Hosted/Dedicated/Private. Interested in LangChain/LlamaIndex examples, gateway proxy patterns, and observability hooks.

[00:00] Maya: Hey everyone thanks for joining, quick intros, I'm Maya, AE on the Redwood side, Liam is our solutions engineer.
[00:15] Ravi: Hi all, Ravi here, head of ML at Cascade. We're re-evaluating our inference stack for the in-app assistant and some internal search features.
[00:22] Diego: Diego, CTO. Big on reliability and cost predictability.
[00:25] Sophie: Sophie, infra. I'll be doing the network and VPC work.
[00:35] Liam: Great, thanks. High level, we want to understand the integration surface — SDKs, LangChain and LlamaIndex support, how you typically put Redwood behind a gateway or proxy, and rate limiting/quotas. Also observability — token-level cost traces, per-route latency.
[00:48] Ravi: Yeah, and we have some strict latency SLOs for chat (under 400ms median) and a hard cost target for per-conversation tokens.
[00:55] Maya: Understood. A couple quick qualifiers — are you leaning hosted first or you planning to go dedicated/private straight away?
[01:03] Ravi: Prefer hosted to start to move fast, but we need predictability. If dedicated gives consistent tail latency, we might go that route for production. Private only if we hit residency/KMS constraints.
[01:20] Liam: Typical pattern: start hosted for integration and eval, run a dedicated pilot for stable latency and throughput, then decide private if control plane or network isolation required. Dedicated gives reserved GPU pools and predictable throughput, we can also configure autoscale/burst.
[01:38] Sophie: About network — if we go dedicated or private, what's the proxy pattern? We have an internal gateway today that does auth and per-user rate limits.
[01:46] Liam: You can place Redwood behind your gateway or call our API directly. For Private and Dedicated we support VPC peering and private endpoints; many customers deploy an API gateway in front and use short-lived service tokens. For Hosted we recommend our API keys + RBAC, but we can do customer-managed proxies for extra audit trails. Sometimes the proxy does token bucketing and then we handle per-route quotas on our side as a backup.
[02:12] Sophie: Any docs or examples for that?
[02:15] Maya: We'll share our gateway pattern doc and a sample NGINX/envoy config. Also a small repo showing how to integrate with SSO and short-lived tokens.
[02:24] Ravi: On SDKs — we're heavy on Python, using LangChain and LlamaIndex. How first-class are those in Redwood?
[02:31] Liam: We have official SDKs in Python/TS. For LangChain and LlamaIndex we provide connectors and example notebooks. The SDK exposes streaming, function/tool calling, and structured output support. There are example chains that show how to plug in Redwood Client or a proxy wrapper for rate limiting.
[02:48] Ravi: Any caveats with LlamaIndex retrieval augmented generation over embeddings? We use dense vector store + hybrid search.
[02:55] Liam: Works fine. Our embeddings API is compatible with common vector libs; we also have guidance on quantization and batching — for high throughput RAG workloads we recommend batching and prefix KV cache to reduce token compute. For embeddings we have per-embedding unit pricing and suggestions to run offline batch embedding jobs.
[03:18] Diego: For the chat latency, can we control model variants and fallbacks? We want graceful degradation if capacity is constrained.
[03:24] Liam: Yes, routing policies can be configured by model, region, and customer tier. You can set automatic fallback to lower-cost variants, and we support canary rollouts, A/B tests, and automatic fallback policies in the console. We also expose per-route SLAs and tracing hooks so you can see when a fallback occurs.
[03:45] Sophie: Speaking of tracing, what observability hooks do you expose? We'll need token-level cost breakdowns and per-request tracing to tie to our request IDs.
[03:54] Liam: We provide tracing headers you can pass through (x-redwood-trace-id) and integration with OpenTelemetry for spans. The console gives token breakdown by prompt/completion and cost, and you can export logs to your SIEM or our audit log export.
[04:10] Ravi: Security checklist — SOC2, KMS, SSO/SAML, data retention policies?
[04:15] Maya: We're SOC2 Type II; we support customer-managed KMS for Private and Dedicated; hosted customers use our KMS but we offer envelope encryption and BYOK options. SSO/SAML and SCIM provisioning supported, RBAC, session auditing, and per-tenant log export. We'll send the security pack after the call.
[04:34] Diego: Great. For the Dedicated trial, what's a reasonable sizing? We'll run a two-week benchmark with our typical convo mix, about 400 QPS peaks for embeddings and 200 concurrent chat sessions.
[04:45] Liam: We'll recommend a baseline GPU pool based on tokens/sec distributions. I'll run some back-of-envelope numbers but we normally start with a modest Dedicated reservation and allow burst to handle spikes. For your numbers, we'll propose config with 4 x A100 equiv units to start, we can adjust after the first 48 hours of profiling.
[05:05] Sophie: Are there rate limit primitives we need to be aware of? Say we want per-user daily quotas plus app-level quotas.
[05:12] Liam: Redwood supports per-key quotas and per-route throttles; many customers implement per-user quotas at the gateway and enforce broader quotas in Redwood as a safety net. For Dedicated you can also configure higher soft-limits and custom rate limit policies.
[05:27] Ravi: We use LangChain chains that open multiple parallel calls for multi-step pipelines — does Redwood support connection pooling and concurrent stream handling?
[05:34] Liam: Yes — the SDK supports multiplexed streaming over HTTP/2 and web sockets to reduce connection overhead. For heavy parallelism we recommend using our batching configs and prefix caching where possible to reduce duplicated context.
[05:51] Maya: Quick note, sometimes transcripts or model names get munched in auto transcriptions — e.g., 'KV cache' might be transcribed as 'K V cash' — just a heads up.
[05:58] Sophie: (laughs) already happened in our demo notes.

[06:10] — mid call, technical snippet discussion (paraphrased) —
[06:12] Liam: For LangChain, here's a pattern: wrap the Redwood client in a proxy layer that does per-user rate limiting, request enrichment, and adds x-redwood-trace-id. For LlamaIndex we recommend using chunking and a small local cache to avoid re-embedding repeated queries. Also, if you use quantized local model variants in Private, you can offload less sensitive workloads on-prem.

[07:05] Ravi: What about billing transparency? We need to attribute costs to product teams for chargeback.
[07:11] Maya: Console has cost breakdowns per token, per-route, and you can tag requests with metadata (team, project) that shows up in cost reports. We also export cost CSVs for ingestion into your FinOps tools.

[08:00] Sophie: Network firewall topologies — to allow a private endpoint we need a specific CIDR and cert pinning, does Redwood support cert rotation?
[08:08] Liam: Yes, cert rotation and mutual TLS are supported for Private and Dedicated endpoints. We'll provide the exact egress CIDRs for the trial environment.

[09:12] Diego: On the POC — what's the success criteria from Redwood's perspective?
[09:16] Maya: Success would be a validated latency profile meeting your SLOs, integration with LangChain/LlamaIndex demonstrated, and a go/no-go decision on Dedicated vs Hosted for production. Ideally we want to expose any blocking security/network issues early.

[09:35] Ravi: Any gotchas with embedding dimensionality or drift?
[09:40] Liam: Embedding dimensionality is standard; if you switch model families later we can provide migration guidance and re-indexing suggestions. For drift, we recommend periodic evals and Redwood Optimize suggestions for quantization and model recommendations.

[10:05] Sophie: Who will own the onboarding sprint?
[10:09] Maya: We'll have an SE owner (Liam) to lead the technical onboarding and CSM for usage and billing. I'll coordinate the timeline.

[10:22] — interruptions and crosstalk as folks check calendars —

[12:00] Liam: A note on KV cache: our runtime manages the KV cache for autoregressive passthrough; for RAG you can use prefix caching to cut tokens for common contexts. We also expose cache hit metrics.

[15:00] Ravi: If we hit rate limit errors during the trial, what's the typical mitigation?
[15:05] Liam: We'll monitor and temporarily increase soft-limits; also we can advise on batching and concurrent call patterns to avoid spiky bursts.

[18:40] Sophie: For Private deployments, how is KMS integrated? We need HSM level or customer-managed KMS keys for certain data.
[18:47] Maya: For Private we support customer-managed KMS (BYOK) and HSM integrations for key wrapping. We'll include details in the security pack.

[22:10] Diego: Are there reference customers in fintech/healthcare for Private deployments?
[22:15] Maya: Yes, we can share redacted case studies — a couple in payments and a healthcare provider who runs Private. I'll send references.

[28:00] Ravi: Let's talk schedule — we want to kick the Dedicated trial next Monday if possible.
[28:06] Maya: We can target that. Liam can prepare the trial env, Sophie to share firewall rules, and Ravi to send prompts.

[35:00] Sophie: One small detail — our infra team is concerned about head-of-line blocking with long streaming connections.
[35:06] Liam: We recommend an adaptive streaming timeout and chunked responses in the SDK; for high concurrency use HTTP/2 multiplexing or websockets. We'll share implementation patterns.

[40:20] — short demo of example LangChain integration by Liam (live code notes not fully captured) —

[44:30] Ravi: That example looks close to our pipeline. We'll run it against our prompt set during the trial.

[48:00] Diego: Cost controls again — can we set hard stop quotas to prevent runaway bills?
[48:06] Maya: Yes, you can set hard spend limits per project and per-key. For Hosted customers we enforce soft-quota warnings and hard limit options; Dedicated customers have different billing flows but can also put spend caps on API keys.

[50:12] Maya: Recap: Maya to send pricing + security pack + gateway patterns; Liam to prep Dedicated trial instructions + example LangChain notebook; Sophie to send infra diagram/firewall rules; Ravi to send prompt set and evaluation metrics. We'll reconvene after the initial benchmark.
[50:36] Ravi: Sounds good. Thanks everyone.
[50:40] Diego: Thanks, looking forward.
[50:45] Maya: I'll follow up with calendar invites for the trial kickoff and the SE deep-dive.
[50:50] — meeting ends —

Notes about transcript quality: occasional transcription errors for product names, some speaker overlaps, timestamps approximate.
